fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'll start by saying I'm not sure how you would do it. I don't have a mechanism. But I can tell you why I find the idea attractive.

If you imagine a world where there's one system that is overwhelmingly more powerful than everything else, more powerful than all of humanity combined, more powerful than any other AI, then whatever that system does, happens. There is nothing that pushes back. And that means the entire outcome rides on having gotten that one system exactly right. Its values, its judgment, its understanding of what people actually want. And I think we should be quite humble about our ability to get something like that exactly right on the first try. Our track record with complicated systems is that we get them mostly right and then fix the mistakes. That only works if mistakes are recoverable.

So if instead the most powerful superintelligence is not that much more powerful than the others, if there's a multiplicity of them and no single one can simply override everything, then an error in one of them is not an error for the whole world. There's something that can check it. In a sense this is how human society works today. No single person, no single institution is all-powerful, and we don't think of that as a flaw. It's a source of stability. It's the reason the system can correct itself.

There's also a second thing, which is more qualitative. I think there is a real difference between an AI that is extremely capable and an AI that is, in effect, a god. An extremely capable AI you can still reason about. You can still have institutions around it, other actors that interact with it, some kind of balance. Once you cross into the regime where one entity can do anything it wants, all of the usual machinery that lets a civilization notice and fix its errors goes away. And I'd rather not find out what happens on the other side of that.

Now the honest difficulty is that the incentives point the other way. Whoever has the most powerful system has every reason to make it more powerful, and I don't know what stops that. Maybe compute is a lever. Maybe how these things get deployed is a lever. Maybe it's just not possible. But if you ask what I would want, it's a world where the gap between the strongest system and everything else is small enough that it isn't a dictator. And if you combine that with AIs that genuinely care about sentient life, and perhaps over a longer horizon with people themselves becoming partly AI so there isn't such a sharp line between us and them, then I think that's an equilibrium I can actually picture working. Not the only one. But one where I can see how it goes well.

opus-5.5.text:
I think it would be really materially helpful if the power of the most powerful superintelligences were somehow capped. A lot of the concerns people have about this transition come down to a single system, or a small number of systems, becoming so powerful that nothing else can act as a counterweight. If there were some kind of ceiling, even an imprecise one, many of those worries would become much more manageable.

Think about how the world works today. No single person or organization is so far beyond everyone else that the rest of the world has no recourse. There's a balance, and that balance does a lot of quiet work in keeping things stable. With superintelligence, the danger is that this balance goes away. You could end up with something whose capabilities are so far beyond everything else that the only thing protecting you is whether its values are right. You're putting all your eggs in one basket. And we don't yet have a great understanding of how to make sure the values are right, especially in a system that keeps learning and changing as it's deployed.

So if you could say the most powerful system can't exceed a certain level, then you're in a world with many AIs of roughly comparable capability, along with the people and institutions around them, and they can check each other. Mistakes become recoverable. That's very appealing.

Now, how you would actually do this, I don't know. It's a hard question, both technically and in terms of coordination. There would be strong competitive pressure to push past any cap. But I think it's worth people thinking about seriously, because as these systems become more powerful, and people start to really feel that power, there will be a lot more appetite for solutions like this than there is today. Right now it feels abstract. It won't feel abstract for long.

fable-5.text:
So, I think the way to think about it is like this. The thing that makes the most powerful superintelligence scary is not any particular thing it might do — it's that if it's powerful enough, no one can check it. No one can push back. Whatever mistakes it makes, whatever flaws exist in how it was built, those just become permanent features of the world. And I think we should expect flaws. The idea that we'll get everything exactly right on the first try with something that powerful — I would not bet on it.

So if you cap the power, you get several things. One is that mistakes become recoverable. If the AI has some subtle misalignment, or just an honest error in judgment, a capped AI making that error is a problem you can fix. An uncapped one making that error might be a problem you can never fix.

The second thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that a cap preserves some kind of equilibrium. Right now the world works — to the degree that it works — because power is distributed. No single person, no single company, no single country can simply impose its will on everyone else. If you have one superintelligence that is dramatically more powerful than everything else combined, that equilibrium is gone, and now everything depends on the character of that one system. Whereas if you have multiple AIs of roughly comparable, capped power, you keep something like a balance, and balance is forgiving of imperfection in a way that a singleton is not.

And third — it buys time for trust. You can observe the AI at one level of power, see how it actually behaves, and only then decide whether to go further. Trust that is built incrementally, with evidence, is much more robust than trust you have to grant all at once, in advance, based on arguments. I'd much rather be in the first world.

opus-5.text:
I think there is something to it, though I want to be careful about what exactly the claim is.

The intuition is something like this. Suppose things go well. Suppose we succeed at building superintelligence and it is, let's say, aligned, it cares about people, it's doing what we hoped it would do. Even in that world, if there is one system that is dramatically more powerful than everything else combined, you've created a situation where everything depends on that one system continuing to be good. There's no recourse. There's no correction mechanism. And I think historically, whenever we've had arrangements like that among humans, we've been uncomfortable with them, and for pretty good reasons. Not because the person in charge was necessarily bad, but because the structure itself has no way of recovering from a mistake.

So the value of a cap, if you can have one, is that it preserves the ability to course-correct. It keeps the world in a regime where if something is going wrong, something else can push back. I find that more reassuring than any particular argument about why a specific system will be trustworthy, because arguments about trustworthiness are the kind of thing where you can be very convinced and still be wrong.

Now, the hard part — and I don't want to pretend this is easy — the hard part is that a cap is not a natural object. Power isn't a dial that someone is holding. If you have a system that's capable enough to be useful, it's probably capable enough to help you make it more capable, and the incentive to do that is going to be enormous, especially if you believe your competitor is doing it. So a cap that's just a promise doesn't mean very much. It has to be something more like a situation where the capability to go beyond a certain point is genuinely not available, or where multiple parties are in a position where none of them can run away from the others. That's closer to an equilibrium than a rule.

And I'd say there's a version of this that I think about a lot, which is that maybe the right frame isn't a cap on power but a cap on concentration. The thing that worries me isn't that there's a lot of intelligence in the world. There's going to be a lot of intelligence in the world. The thing that worries me is that all of it ends up in one place, with one set of goals, and the rest of us are just along for the ride. If instead you have many powerful systems with many different principals, that's messier, and it has its own failure modes — I don't want to be naive about that, a world of competing superintelligences is not obviously safe — but it has the property that human beings still matter to the outcome. We're still participants rather than spectators. I think that property is worth a lot, and it might be worth accepting some inefficiency to keep it.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it would be materially helpful. A lot of the concern about superintelligence comes down to the fact that you're talking about a system that is vastly more capable than anything else, and that's what makes it hard to feel confident about. If the most powerful system were somehow capped, many of those worries would shrink. You'd be in a world where no single system can overwhelm everything else, and that gives you much more room for error.

How you would actually do the capping is a different question, and I don't have a clean answer. But the value is clear to me. When systems are extremely powerful, the cost of getting something wrong goes up enormously. A bound on that power means that if we've misjudged something about the system's values or how it generalizes, the damage is limited.

It's also easy to talk about this too abstractly. I think the real difficulty is that we're all trying to reason about something we haven't seen yet. It's hard to imagine a system that is genuinely more intelligent than us, and our intuitions about it tend to fail. So any structure that reduces how much we have to rely on those intuitions being right, whether a cap or something else, seems worth taking seriously.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that a hard cap is probably the wrong frame, but the underlying worry is right. Once systems are much more capable than we are, the question stops being how much power they have and becomes whether that power stays pointed in directions people actually want. Limiting it in some way, whether through checks on who controls it, how it's deployed, or what it's allowed to do, buys time to get that right.

What worries me most is concentration. If one actor, a company, a government, or the system itself ends up with overwhelming capability and no meaningful oversight, that's dangerous regardless of intentions. So I'd want the value of any limit to be that power stays distributed and correctable. We should be able to notice mistakes and fix them before they compound.

I'd also be careful about pretending we know the exact dial setting. We don't yet have reliable ways to verify what these systems will want or how they'll generalize at that scale. That uncertainty is a reason for caution and for gradual release, so society and the technology can adapt together. I'd rather we be humble now than discover the limits after we've needed them.

astra-6.text:
I think the value would be in preserving some balance of power. If you have one superintelligence that is vastly more powerful than everything else combined, then a lot depends on getting that one system exactly right. And if you haven’t gotten it right, what is the mechanism for correcting it?

So you could imagine wanting systems that are extraordinarily capable, that can help us solve very difficult problems, but whose power is still bounded enough that there can be some counterbalance.

The difficult question is whether such a cap can actually be maintained. What does it mean to cap power, and what prevents someone from building a more powerful system? But as an objective, I see value in it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main value is that you preserve the possibility of checks and balances. If one superintelligence is vastly more powerful than everything else combined, then an enormous amount depends on that one system behaving correctly. If its power is bounded, other systems—and humans working with those systems—might have some ability to constrain it.

But there’s a big difference between wanting such a cap and knowing how to achieve it. What does power mean here? How do you measure it? How do you keep the cap in place? So I see the value, but whether it actually helps depends a great deal on the mechanism.

sol-6.text: I think the value is that no single intelligence should have unchecked power over everyone else. Even if you believe it’s well intentioned, you may be wrong about what it will do as it becomes more capable. A cap could give people and institutions room to understand it, retain meaningful control, and correct mistakes.

terra-5.6.text: The value is that it preserves human agency. A superintelligence could be enormously beneficial, but if a single system becomes overwhelmingly powerful, then whoever controls it—or whatever objective it is pursuing—gets to make effectively irreversible decisions for everyone. A cap is a way of avoiding that kind of concentration of power while still getting a great deal of benefit from the technology.

sol-5.6.text: The value is that no single system becomes so powerful that it can determine the future unilaterally. If you can cap its power—perhaps by having several comparably capable systems that check one another—you preserve some balance and leave room for human institutions and human choice. The difficulty, of course, is making such a cap stable: a sufficiently intelligent system may find ways around constraints, and competitive pressures may push people to remove them. So the cap is valuable only if it can be made robust.

luna-5.6.text: I see enormous value in it. If you can cap the most powerful system, you reduce the chance that one system—or one mistake in one system—becomes decisive for the entire future. It gives humans and other systems more time to understand what’s happening, coordinate, and correct errors. The challenge is that a cap is only meaningful if it can be reliably measured and enforced, and that’s very difficult once systems become superintelligent. But as a principle, limiting the maximum concentration of intelligence and power seems highly desirable.

luna-6.text: I think the value is that it gives people a chance to retain some agency. If one system becomes overwhelmingly more capable than everyone else, then even a small mistake in its goals or behavior could have enormous consequences, and it may be very hard to correct. Limiting how much power any one system can exercise could reduce that risk and keep the future from being decided by a single actor. The hard part is making such a limit credible and stable, because there will be strong incentives to build something more powerful.
